text: Bicep's first-look lesson showed you one resource block declaring one resource. Real Azure environments rarely stay that simple — you need three storage accounts, not one, or a security group that only exists in some deployments. This lesson covers the Bicep syntax that handles both: the for expression for looping over an array of similar resources, the if keyword for deploying a resource conditionally, and how Bicep's symbolic names let it infer dependencies automatically, without you ever writing dependsOn by hand.

The for expression expands one resource block into several real resources, one per entry in an array. Declare a storageNames array parameter holding three names, then write resource storageAccts '...' = [for name in storageNames: { ... }], and Bicep deploys all three storage accounts from that single block — no copy-pasting three nearly-identical resource declarations. Need the array index too, for numbering something or pairing it with a second array? Write for (name, i) in storageNames instead, and both the value and its position are available inside the loop body.

Some resources should only exist in certain deployments — a Network Security Group built only in a guarded environment, a bastion host only when a parameter asks for one. The if keyword goes right after the equals sign on a resource block: resource nsg '...' = if (deployNsg) { ... }. When deployNsg evaluates to false, Bicep never submits that resource to Azure Resource Manager at all — it's skipped entirely, not created and then removed. For and if can even combine on the same resource, looping over an array while filtering which entries actually deploy.

storageAccts and nsg in those examples are symbolic names — labels you chose for referencing a resource elsewhere in the same Bicep file. Azure never sees them; they exist purely for the compiler. Write parent: storageAccts[0] inside a child blobService resource, and Bicep recognizes that reference, automatically compiling both the correct scope and a dependsOn into the resulting ARM JSON, in the right order, with zero manual dependsOn syntax. You only reach for an explicit dependsOn when a real dependency exists that no reference in your file reveals, which is the rare case, not the norm.

That's real Bicep syntax beyond a first look — loops, conditionals, and automatic dependency inference from symbolic names. Next lesson stays in Bicep but moves from syntax to structure: breaking a deployment into reusable modules, and supplying different values per environment with parameter files.
